prompt: Why should daily prices not be shuffled at random before they are split into training and test parts?

options.text: Random shuffles give a fairer test, because every day has an equal chance of landing in either part
Shuffling mixes later prices into the training part, so the choice learns from prices that come after the test days
Shuffling makes the data smaller, so the test runs faster
Shuffling only matters for intraday data, not daily data

explanations.a: Random shuffles break the time order. The training part then holds prices from after some test days, which leaks the future into the past.
explanations.c: Shuffling does not change how much data there is. The problem is the order of the dates.
explanations.d: Time order matters for any price series. Shuffled daily data causes the same leak.

prompt: Hypothetical. Ten years of daily prices, 2016 to 2025. Training window 3 years, test window 1 year, rolling forward by 1 year. How many test windows are there?
solution: Each window covers 3 + 1 = 4 years. The test years run from 2019 to 2025. Count: 2025 - 2019 + 1 = 7. Check: the window starts run from 2016 to 2022, which is also 7 starts. Answer: 7.

prompt: You tested a rule on 2023 and then changed one stop distance. You tested again on 2023 and the result looked better. What is 2023 now?

options.text: Still out-of-sample, because you changed only one number
Still out-of-sample, because you looked at it only twice
In-sample, because a choice was made using it
A third kind of data that is neither in-sample nor out-of-sample

explanations.a: A single change still counts. The period was used to choose a setting, so it is no longer a clean test.
explanations.b: The number of looks does not matter here. The problem is that a choice was made using the period.
explanations.d: There are only two parts in this split: in-sample and out-of-sample. 2023 has been used for choosing, so it is in-sample.

prompt: What does a walk-forward run tell you?

options.text: It proves the strategy works.
It shows how the rule's choices held up across several separate test windows, which is one more piece of evidence.
It removes all bias from the test.
It shows that the test period can be used to choose settings.

explanations.a: A walk-forward run is evidence, not proof. Many things can still go wrong after the test.
explanations.c: Walk-forward does not remove look-ahead bias, survivorship bias or overfitting. Each needs its own check.
explanations.d: Using the test period to choose settings makes it in-sample. That breaks the test.

prompt: Hypothetical. A split has a training window from 2016 to 2019. Its test window starts in 2018. What is wrong with this split?

options.text: Nothing. Test windows may overlap training windows.
The test window starts before the training window ends, so the test uses data that the settings were learned from.
The training window is too long.
The test window is too short to count.

explanations.a: Overlap means the test uses data that the choice already used. That is not out-of-sample testing.
explanations.c: The length of the training window is not the problem. The overlap is the problem.
explanations.d: A short test window can be weak evidence, but the main fault here is that the windows overlap.

prompt: Read this plan: 'I split the data 60/40 by time. I picked the stop distance using the last 40 percent. Then I tested the rule on that same 40 percent.' Which part is wrong?

options.text: The 60/40 split by time
Using the last 40 percent to pick the stop distance, which makes that part in-sample
Testing the rule at all
Nothing is wrong

explanations.a: A split by time is correct. The dates stay in order.
explanations.c: Testing is the right step. The fault is what was done with the test data before the test.
explanations.d: The 40 percent was used to choose, so testing on it does not give an out-of-sample result.
